title: Building AI to accelerate science and improve lives
gist: James Manyika lays out Google's applied-AI portfolio across health, disaster prediction, learning, economic opportunity and language, anchored on hard deployment numbers: AlphaFold's 200 million predicted protein structures used by 4 million researchers in 190 countries, AlphaGenome Atlas mapping all 9 billion single-letter human genetic variants openly, WeatherNext 3 delivering 50% more accurate day-ahead precipitation forecasts, Flood Hub covering 2 billion people in 150+ countries, and a Planetary Prediction Engine that pinpointed 83% of Ebola hotspots in the DRC ahead of time. The strategic tell is the 'missed use' framing — Manyika argues under-deployment of AI is a risk on par with misuse, a policy argument that cuts against precautionary regulation.

themes.theme: Open biology assets and the research moat

insights.claim: Google has mapped all 9 billion possible single-letter genetic changes across the human genome with AlphaGenome Atlas and released it openly to researchers, extending the AlphaFold playbook of giving away the reference dataset in a new biological domain.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Openly released variant-effect maps commoditize a layer that genomics interpretation companies charge for; watch margin pressure on variant-annotation and clinical-interpretation vendors.
insights.quote: We mapped all 9 billion possible single letter genetic changes across the human genome with AlphaGenome Atlas and made it openly available to researchers.
insights.locator: This comes on top of a raft of key AI advances

insights.claim: AlphaFold has predicted all 200 million protein structures known to science and is now used by 4 million researchers across 190 countries, making it de facto public research infrastructure rather than a product.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: 4 million researchers in 190 countries is a distribution footprint that no rival structure-prediction tool can dislodge; it guarantees Google sits upstream of drug-discovery workflows worldwide.
insights.quote: It is now used by 4 million researchers in 190 countries in areas from drug discovery to understanding neglected diseases

insights.claim: Google is stacking its biology models into a chain — AlphaFold for structure, AlphaMissense for disease-causing mutations, and now AlphaGenome Atlas for how genetic variation alters cellular behavior — moving from static structure prediction toward predicting functional consequence.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Function prediction, not structure, is where pharma value sits; a model chain that reaches cellular behavior puts Google adjacent to target validation, the most expensive failure point in drug development.

insights.claim: Google has open-sourced DeepConsensus, DeepVariant and DeepPolisher, which over the last decade contributed to completing the human genome, drafting the first pangenome, and ongoing work with the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Free, best-in-class variant callers lock the genomics tooling layer to Google's stack while sequencer makers and cloud providers monetize the throughput around it.
insights.locator: Tools for scientists and health practitioners

insights.claim: Co-Scientist is being used to generate and validate novel hypotheses — including identifying new therapeutic applications for existing drugs in acute myeloid leukemia — positioning AI inside the hypothesis-generation step of the scientific method rather than only the analysis step.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Drug repurposing is the fastest path to monetizable AI-derived IP because it skips early safety work; watch for named repurposing candidates entering trials as the first real validation.
insights.locator: Tools for scientists and health practitioners

insights.claim: A breast cancer study with Imperial College London and the UK's NHS found AI detected 25% of interval cancers previously missed in mammograms of 175,000 women — a measured miss-recovery rate on a large real-world cohort, not a benchmark result.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Recovering a quarter of interval cancers is the kind of number that moves national screening procurement; the NHS is the reference customer other public health systems follow.
insights.quote: showed AI can detect 25% of interval cancers previously missed in mammograms of 175,000 women

insights.claim: Roughly 40% of people infected with tuberculosis worldwide go undiagnosed, and Google's chest X-ray model, deployed via Nexus Intelligence, has screened over 25,000 x-rays across 40 locations in six nations — a large unmet need paired with a still-small deployment footprint.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: 25,000 x-rays against a 40% global undiagnosed rate shows the bottleneck is deployment and imaging hardware, not model quality — the investable layer is distribution partners, not the model.
insights.quote: where ~40% of infected people worldwide go undiagnosed

insights.claim: Google's diabetic retinopathy model has supported more than 1.15 million screenings globally with a stated plan to reach 6 million over the next decade, implying a deliberately modest roughly 5x scaling ambition over ten years.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: A 10-year 5x target for a mature deployed model is a candid signal that healthcare AI scaling is gated by clinical workflow and regulation, not algorithms — temper expectations on health-AI revenue ramps.
insights.quote: has supported more than 1.15 million screenings globally, with plans to expand to 6 million over the next decade

insights.claim: Google is pushing diagnosis onto commodity consumer hardware — using everyday smartphones and wearables for early detection of cardiovascular disease, insulin resistance, hypertension, loss of pulse, and passive heart rate monitoring.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Moving screening onto phones already in pockets bypasses clinical capital expenditure entirely and is the single largest addressable-market expander in this portfolio — a direct threat to dedicated diagnostic device makers.

insights.claim: AMIE is being advanced toward longitudinal disease management with prospective real-world evidence, collaborations including Beth Israel Deaconess Center, and a first-of-its-kind nationwide trial in real-world care settings — moving clinical AI from retrospective benchmarks to prospective trials.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: A nationwide prospective trial is the regulatory prerequisite for reimbursable AI care; the readout is the event to watch for whether diagnostic AI gets billing codes.
insights.locator: Tools for scientists and health practitioners

insights.claim: Google frames AMIE as assisting frontline care providers and freeing doctors for patient time rather than replacing clinicians — the standard augmentation framing used to defuse professional and regulatory resistance to clinical AI.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Augmentation framing determines which budget line pays; if AI is a physician tool rather than a substitute it is sold into IT budgets, which are far smaller than labor budgets.
insights.quote: AMIE assists those providing care on the frontlines — freeing up doctors to spend more time with their patients.
insights.locator: Tools for scientists and health practitioners

themes.theme: Weather and crisis prediction at national scale

insights.claim: WeatherNext 3 delivers 50% more accurate precipitation forecasts a day or more ahead and is already deployed in Google products, marking a step change in a domain historically owned by national meteorological agencies.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: A 50% precipitation accuracy gain is directly monetizable in agriculture, energy trading and insurance; it also pressures the commercial weather data incumbents who resell agency output.
insights.quote: our most advanced and accurate global weather model, delivering 50% more accurate precipitation forecasts a day or more ahead

insights.claim: WeatherNext 3 combines real-time satellite observations with AI to produce high-resolution hourly forecasts without immense supercomputing power, which specifically advantages data-sparse regions long underserved by high-resolution forecasting.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Removing the supercomputer dependency destroys the cost structure that made national weather services the only viable providers — the economics of forecasting just shifted to whoever owns the model.
insights.quote: delivering high-resolution, hourly forecasts without immense supercomputing power — a major step forward for data-sparse regions

insights.claim: The Earth AI Planetary Prediction Engine pinpointed 83% of emerging hotspots ahead of time in the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which Google states beat current forecasting systems.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Outperforming incumbent epidemiological forecasting in a live outbreak is the strongest validation datapoint in the article and a template for public-health procurement of AI forecasting.
insights.quote: PPE successfully pinpointed 83% of emerging hotspots ahead of time, beating current forecasting systems.

insights.claim: The Planetary Prediction Engine doubled food security forecasting accuracy at local district level in Nigeria and outperformed traditional models in identifying vulnerable US communities across 21 CDC health indicators, showing the same architecture transfers across crisis types and geographies.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Cross-domain transfer from epidemiology to food security to US public health indicators means one model can address multiple government budgets — a much larger TAM than any single-hazard tool.
insights.quote: In Nigeria, PPE doubled food security forecasting accuracy at the local district level.

insights.claim: The Planetary Prediction Engine is described as an autonomous AI system driven by simple language instructions that predicts disease outbreaks, food shortages and climate risks almost instantly — an agentic interface layered on top of fused global health, food security and socioeconomic data.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Natural-language querying over fused planetary datasets collapses the analyst layer between data and decision — the disruption target is consultancies and specialist modeling firms, not software.
insights.quote: an autonomous AI system that uses simple language instructions to almost instantly predict global crises

insights.claim: Jamaican authorities used WeatherNext to accurately predict Hurricane Melissa's path, which the article says secured early disaster funding and enabled emergency preparations long before landfall — tying forecast quality directly to the release of capital.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Forecasts that unlock anticipatory disaster financing create a paying customer in multilateral and sovereign disaster funds — a real revenue channel beyond consumer weather apps.
insights.quote: authorities in Jamaica used WeatherNext to accurately predict Hurricane Melissa’s path, securing early disaster funding

insights.claim: Google's Flood Hub forecasts now cover both riverine and flash floods for 2 billion people across more than 150 countries, and its 2025 monsoon predictions reached 38 million farmers in India.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Reaching 2 billion people and 38 million Indian farmers makes Google a de facto piece of national agricultural and civil-defense infrastructure — a soft-power position with real regulatory leverage.
insights.quote: have grown to cover 2 billion people across more than 150 countries in areas at risk for significant flood events

insights.claim: Google generated more than 520 crisis alerts on Google Search in 2025 delivering wildfire information to over 75 million users, and its wildfire boundary prediction now covers the US plus 33 other countries with a FireSat satellite constellation in development.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Search as the alert delivery channel is a moat competitors cannot buy; the FireSat constellation signals Google moving into owned space-based sensing, a capital-intensive vertical integration.
insights.quote: we generated more than 520 crisis alerts on Google Search that provided timely wildfire information to over 75 million users around the world

insights.claim: Google's Earthquake Alert system warned millions of people in Venezuela ahead of an earthquake in the months before publication, extending Android-based early warning into a country with limited seismic infrastructure.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Crowd-sensed earthquake warning using Android handsets is essentially free infrastructure that displaces national seismic networks in emerging markets — a durable government-relations asset.

insights.claim: Global learning outcomes have declined over the last two decades across 81 countries despite 90% primary enrollment and roughly 87% primary completion — Google uses this quality-versus-access gap as the entry wedge for AI in education.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Declining outcomes on near-universal enrollment means the spend shifts from building schools to improving instruction quality — the budget line AI tutoring products are aimed at.
insights.quote: Global learning outcomes have declined over the last two decades across 81 countries.
insights.locator: Learning is the bedrock of economic and societal progress

insights.claim: Google partnered with ISTE+ASCD to provide AI literacy training to all 6 million educators in the United States, a teacher-first channel strategy that seeds adoption through the professional body rather than through district software procurement.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Owning the training standard for every US teacher is a cheap way to make Google's tools the default in classrooms before any procurement decision is made — a structural disadvantage for edtech rivals.
insights.quote: we have partnered with ISTE+ASCD to provide AI literacy training to all 6 million educators in the U.S.
insights.locator: Tackling challenges and focusing on responsible design

insights.claim: Google openly lists accuracy, safety, critical thinking, cheating and learning loss as real risks of AI in education and states its design principle is teachers in the lead with AI as the assistant, conceding 'we still have much to work through together.'
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Explicit risk acknowledgement from the vendor is unusual and signals expected regulatory scrutiny of AI in schools; the teacher-in-the-lead framing is the compliance posture to watch.
insights.quote: AI presents real challenges for learning, including questions on accuracy, safety, critical thinking, cheating, and learning loss.
insights.locator: Tackling challenges and focusing on responsible design

themes.theme: Labor market thesis and the measurement layer

insights.claim: Manyika's explicit labor framework is three-way — some jobs decline, some grow, and many more change as AI assists workers — with the emphasis on the third bucket, a deliberately less alarming framing than net-displacement narratives.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: The 'most jobs change' framing is the intellectual foundation for arguing against aggressive AI labor regulation; expect it to anchor Google's policy submissions.
insights.quote: Some jobs are likely to decline, some jobs will grow, and many more jobs will change as AI increasingly assists workers.

insights.claim: Manyika states plainly that the economic benefits of AI are neither automatic nor guaranteed, a hedge that undercuts the productivity-boom consensus even while Google markets the technology.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: When a vendor's own SVP disclaims automatic productivity gains, investors underwriting AI-driven margin expansion should treat realization risk as material, not tail.
insights.quote: The economic benefits of AI are neither automatic nor guaranteed.

insights.claim: Google launched the AI & Economy ATLAS to supply empirical data on how people actually use AI at work and in daily life, translating it into an interactive open-access experience — an attempt to own the measurement layer of the AI economic debate.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Whoever supplies the adoption statistics frames the policy conversation; ATLAS numbers will likely become the cited baseline in labor-impact regulation and in sell-side AI adoption models.

insights.claim: Manyika argues AI's value lies not in what the technology does on its own but in how people choose to use it and what they build with it — an implicit deflection of responsibility for outcomes onto adopters.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: This framing shifts the value-capture argument toward application builders and adopters rather than model vendors, which is notable coming from a model vendor.
insights.quote: Its true value isn’t in what it does on its own, but in how people choose to use it and what they build with it
insights.locator: Across the economy, AI can drive innovation

insights.claim: Google has spent more than $1 billion globally on training and skilling, reaching over 100 million people with digital and AI skills, and concedes that more tailored worker assistance and transition support will likely be needed.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: $1 billion for 100 million people is about $10 per person — the admission that tailored transition support is still needed signals where public spending, not corporate spending, will have to go.
insights.quote: Google has provided more than $1 billion globally in training and skilling initiatives, helping over 100 million people gain essential digital and AI skills

insights.claim: Google points to Pomelli for small-business custom marketing campaigns and the Gemini Enterprise App for consolidating complex regional sales data across product lines, indicating the SMB monetization surface is workflow apps rather than raw model access.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Named SMB applications show Google moving up the stack into the application layer where SaaS incumbents sit, not staying neutral as an infrastructure supplier.

insights.claim: Google technologies now support more than 300 languages spoken by 7 billion people, which Google quantifies as 86% of the global population, while Translate handles around 1 trillion words a month for more than 1 billion people.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: A trillion words a month is a proprietary multilingual usage signal that no competitor can replicate and that directly feeds model improvement — the underrated part of Google's AI moat.
insights.quote: Google technologies now support more than 300 languages, spoken by 7 billion people — representing 86% of the global population.
insights.locator: Today, we reached a significant milestone

insights.claim: Google is sourcing low-resource language data through named academic partnerships — Makerere University, University of Ghana and Digital Umuganda for an open dataset covering 27 African languages spoken by over 100 million people, and IISc Bangalore with ARTPARK on Project Vaani for 109 Indic languages.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Field-collected speech data in Africa and India is the scarce input for the next billion users; university partnerships are cheaper and more defensible than licensing deals.

insights.claim: Google has released a sign-language-to-text model for sign-to-text dictation, pushing accessibility beyond spoken language into a modality that requires visual rather than audio understanding.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Sign-to-text requires real-time video understanding on-device, so shipping it is evidence of multimodal edge-inference capability with applications well beyond accessibility.

themes.theme: Policy framing: 'missed use' and the collaboration model

insights.claim: Manyika introduces 'missed use' as a named risk category alongside misuse — arguing that failing to apply AI where it would help is itself harmful and can worsen existing societal gaps, a framing that converts under-deployment into a moral cost.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: This is the sharpest policy move in the article: it reframes precautionary regulation as an active harm, and will likely recur in Google's arguments against restrictive AI rules.
insights.quote: it is important to avoid the risk of missed use — that is, not applying AI in places and communities where it would provide benefit

insights.claim: Google simultaneously flags the need for detection, reporting and mitigation tools for chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear misuse, pairing CBRN risk acknowledgement with its pro-deployment argument to preempt the strongest objection to open scientific AI releases.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: CBRN safeguards are the specific condition regulators will attach to openly released biology models; the compliance cost of those safeguards is the hidden expense in open-science AI strategies.

insights.claim: Google has given more than $1 billion across 1,700+ research institutions worldwide since 2006, using academic grant-making as a structural channel for both talent access and scientific legitimacy.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Two decades of grants across 1,700 institutions builds influence over the academic research agenda that shapes future AI policy evidence — a slow-compounding, hard-to-replicate asset.
insights.quote: Google has given more than $1 billion across 1,700+ research institutions worldwide since 2006
insights.locator: That’s why as part of our longstanding commitment

insights.claim: Manyika invokes Nobel laureate Joel Mokyr's technology-science feedback loop and claims AI is the most powerful engine for that loop ever built, framing AI as a fundamental driver of long-run growth rather than a product cycle.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Mokyr's feedback-loop framing is the standard intellectual case for structurally higher trend productivity growth from AI; it is the argument underlying elevated long-duration valuations in the sector.
insights.quote: a positive feedback loop that can keep growing with no end in sight.
insights.locator: As Nobel laureate Joel Mokyr noted

insights.claim: Google has scaled AI research to cut aviation's climate impact and is already applying it in the UK in collaboration with the government and in Asia, showing the same applied-science playbook being run in an industrial-emissions context.
insights.speaker: James Manyika
insights.so_what: Government co-deployment in aviation climate mitigation positions Google inside contrail and emissions policy, an area heading toward regulatory mandates in the EU and UK.
insights.quote: We scaled AI research to help cut the climate impact of aviation — this is already being applied in the U.K.
insights.locator: This comes on top of a raft of key AI advances
